title_ar: حكم الكف عن قص الشعر و الأظافر في عشر ذي الحجة
title_en: The Ruling on Refraining from Cutting the Hair and Nails During the Ten Days of Dhu al-Hijjah
body_ar:
بالنسبة لمن لا أضحية له و لأفراد الأسرة الذين سيضحي عنهم كافلهم يجوز لهم أن يأخذوا من الشعر و الأظفار متى شاءوا باتفاق العلماء.

أما بالنسبة لمن يريد أن يضحي بنفسه فقد اختلف الفقهاء فيه بين الحرمة والكراهة والإباحة:

فرأى الحنابلة وبعض الشافعية أنه يحرم عليه الأخذ من الشعر و الأظافر حتى يذكي أضحيته

و رأى الحنفية أنه يجوز له ذلك من غير كراهة

و رأى المالكية والشافعية أنه يكره له ذلك وأن ترك الأخذ من الشعر و الأظافر مندوب وليس بواجب ،

والأصل في ذلك ما روى الإمام مسلم عن أم سلمة -رضي اللَّه عنها- أنَّ النبيَّﷺ قال: «إذا رأيتم هلاَلَ ذي الحجة، وأرادَ أحَدُكم أَنْ يَضَحِّيَ فَلْيُمْسكْ عن شَعرِه وأظْفَارهِ»، وفي رواية: «فَلاَ يَأْخُذَنَّ شَعرا وَلاَ يَقْلِمَنَّ ظُفرا»

وهذا نهي والنهي إذا لم يقتض التحريم حمل على الكراهة قال الشيخ خليل: "و(ندب) ترك حلق وقلمٍ لِمُضَحٍّ عشرَ ذي الحجة"، وإنما ندب للتشبه بالحاج،

واستدل المالكية والشافعية على أن النهي للكراهة وليس للتحريم بما روى الإمام مالك والشيخان عن عائشة -رضي اللَّه عنها- قالت: «أنا فَتَلْتُ قلائد بُدْنِ رسول اللهﷺ بِيَدَىَّ، ثم أشعرها وقلدها، ثم بعث بها إلى البيت وأقام بالمدينة، فما حرم عليه شيء كان له حِلاًّ»، وفي رواية: «ثم بعث بهاﷺ مع أبي»؛ أي مع أبي بكر رضي الله عنه في السنة التاسعة من الهجرة

ومعناه: فما حرم عليه شيء من محظورات الإحرام؛ من النساء، والطيب، وإزالة الشعث، وحلق الشعر، وتقليم الأظفار، وغير ذلك مما أحله الله...

والله أعلم
body_en:
As for one who has no Eid sacrifice (uḍḥiyah), and for the members of a household on whose behalf the one who supports them will be sacrificing, it is permissible for them to cut their hair and their nails whenever they wish, by the agreement of the scholars.

As for one who intends to perform the sacrifice himself, the jurists have differed over him between forbiddenness, dislikedness and permissibility:

The Hanbalis and some of the Shafi'is held that it is forbidden (ḥarām) for him to cut his hair or his nails until he has slaughtered his sacrificial animal.

The Hanafis held that it is permissible (jāʾiz) for him to do so, without its being disliked.

The Malikis and the Shafi'is held that it is disliked (makrūh) for him, and that refraining from cutting the hair and the nails is recommended (mandūb) and not obligatory (wājib).

The basis of this is what Imam Muslim narrated from Umm Salamah (may God be pleased with her), that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "When you see the crescent of Dhu al-Hijjah, and one of you intends to sacrifice, let him refrain from his hair and his nails"; and in another narration: "let him not cut any hair nor clip any nail."

This is a prohibitive command, and a prohibitive command, when it does not entail forbiddenness, is taken to convey dislikedness. Sheikh Khalil said: "And it is recommended (nadb) for one who is to sacrifice to leave off shaving and clipping during the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah." It is recommended only in order to resemble the pilgrim.

The Malikis and the Shafi'is argued that the prohibition conveys dislikedness and not forbiddenness by what Imam Malik and the two Sheikhs [al-Bukhari and Muslim] narrated from Aisha (may God be pleased with her), who said: "I plaited the garlands of the Messenger of God's sacrificial camels with my own hands; then he marked them and garlanded them, then sent them to the House while he himself stayed in Medina, and nothing that had been lawful for him became forbidden to him"; and in another narration: "then he (peace and blessings be upon him) sent them with my father" — that is, with Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him), in the ninth year of the Hijrah.

Its meaning is: nothing of the prohibited acts of the consecrated state of pilgrimage (iḥrām) became forbidden to him — not women, nor perfume, nor removing dishevelment, nor shaving the hair, nor clipping the nails, nor anything else of what God has made lawful…

And God knows best.

flags.arabic: وهذا نهي والنهي إذا لم يقتض التحريم حمل على الكراهة ... والله أعلم
flags.context: the closing two-thirds of the answer, which sets out the evidence for the Maliki and Shafi'i position and then ends
options: treat the Maliki and Shafi'i position as the one the Sheikh adopts, without saying so on the page
display the record with a note that the text sets out the positions and their evidence but never states in the first person which the Sheikh holds
withhold pending confirmation from the Sheikh's office
flags.note: The answer reports four positions — forbidden (Hanbalis, some Shafi'is), permissible without dislike (Hanafis), disliked and refraining recommended (Malikis, Shafi'is) — and then devotes the rest of the text to the evidence for the third, quoting Khalil's Mukhtaṣar approvingly. It never says 'and this is what I hold'. Style guide section 10 warns that a reader will take the last-stated position for the Sheikh's fatwa. Here the last-stated position happens to be his own school's, so the risk is lower than in the cases section 10 contemplates and critical_for_display has NOT been set; but the English states no preference the Arabic does not state, and the display should not present the Maliki position as his ruling without confirmation.

flags.arabic: يحرم عليه الأخذ من الشعر و الأظافر ... أنه يجوز له ذلك ... أنه يكره له ذلك
options: keep each ruling attached to the school that holds it, as done here
flags.note: Recorded rather than uncertain: every ruling word in this answer belongs to a reported school position, not to the Sheikh in his own voice. The fixed mapping of style guide section 3 has been applied to each — ḥarām 'forbidden', jāʾiz 'permissible', makrūh 'disliked', mandūb 'recommended', wājib 'obligatory' — and each remains visibly attributed. Note that جائز here qualifies an act, so the legal sense applies and the kalām exemption of section 8 does not.

translator_notes: الشيخان in hadith usage means al-Bukhari and Muslim; the English supplies the names in square brackets, since 'the two Sheikhs' would be opaque.
الشيخ خليل is Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Jundi, whose Mukhtaṣar is the standard Maliki manual; the quotation is from it. The name is given in body text without diacritics per the house style.
بُدْن are the camels (and cattle) driven for sacrifice; 'sacrificial camels' is used because the point of the report is the marking and garlanding of the animals.
إزالة الشعث is removing dishevelment — the grooming a pilgrim in iḥrām abstains from — and is rendered literally, since it is one item in a list of the prohibited acts of iḥrām (maḥẓūrāt).
The Arabic uses both الأظفار and الأظافر for 'nails' within the same text; both are correct plurals and neither has been altered.
The ellipsis before والله أعلم is in the source and has been kept.
Classified fatwa on the corrected test: a real question and a real body of ruling are present, notwithstanding the short length.
